passage: The monsoon had turned the lane to red mud, so Irfan, who ran the tea stall by the bus stop, kept an eye on Jomon while Jomon's mother sold bananas next door. Jomon, not yet two, pushed himself up on the stall's bench, let go, and stamped three steps towards the drain. Irfan scooped him back. Jomon wriggled down, climbed onto the low stone step, jumped off with both feet, and laughed at his own splash.

qa.q: Where did Irfan run his tea stall?
qa.a: By the bus stop.

qa.q: What does Jomon's laugh after the splash suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed delighted and proud of jumping off the step by himself, not upset about being scooped back. 😊

qa.q: How could Irfan support Jomon's climbing and jumping safely?
qa.a: He could let him keep practising on the low step while blocking only the real danger, the drain, instead of stopping all movement.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to watch Jomon while running the stall?
qa.a: He has to split his attention between customers and a toddler who suddenly moves fast, so he stays alert and quick to act.

grounding: Shows a toddler standing, walking, climbing a step and jumping, with an adult keeping him away from danger.

passage: Noa had just learned to run, which mostly meant falling forward fast. At the playground in Rotterdam she ran at the pigeons, tumbled on the rubber mat, and lay still for a second, checking her mother's face. Dalia smiled and said, "Up you get." Noa rolled onto her knees, pushed on her hands, stood, and set off again, arms wide. At the climbing frame she hauled one foot onto the lowest bar and stayed there, grunting.

qa.q: What did Noa run at in the playground?
qa.a: She ran at the pigeons.

qa.q: Why did Noa check her mother's face after she tumbled?
qa.a: She was unsure whether the fall was scary, so she looked to Dalia to decide how to feel, and the smile reassured her.

qa.q: What small step would help Noa with the climbing frame?
qa.a: Dalia could stand close and let her keep trying the lowest bar, steadying her hips rather than lifting her up.

qa.q: How might Dalia see Noa's many falls?
qa.a: She seems to see them as a normal part of learning to run, so she stays calm instead of rushing in.

grounding: Shows a toddler running, falling, getting back up and starting to climb.

passage: I'm Tanuja, from the house opposite. During the Pongal holidays our lane was covered in kolams, and Harsha, who is almost two, spent the whole week trying to cross them. On the first day he crawled right through the rice flour. By the third day he was stepping carefully between the lines, arms out, stopping to wobble. On the last morning he ran the length of the lane to his grandmother. Maybe he was proud; I only know he didn't look down once.

qa.q: What covered the lane during the Pongal holidays?
qa.a: Kolams covered the lane.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling when he ran the length of the lane?
qa.a: Probably confident and pleased with himself, though Tanuja can only guess from how he never looked down.

qa.q: How could Harsha's family support his walking during a festival week like this?
qa.a: They could give him space to practise on the open lane while guiding him around fresh kolams, rather than carrying him everywhere.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see the change across the week?
qa.a: Tanuja notices him move from crawling through the flour to stepping between lines and then running, a clear gain in balance and control.

grounding: Shows a toddler's large-muscle skills growing from crawling to careful stepping to running over one festival week.

passage: Saurabh put a small heap of boiled peas on the steel plate and waited. His son Deepak, eighteen months old, first slapped the heap with his whole palm, and peas flew under the sofa. Then he stopped, pinched one pea between his thumb and one finger, and carried it slowly to his mouth. He chewed, looked at his father, and reached for another. Twenty minutes later the peas were gone, and so was Saurabh's plan to finish lunch quickly.

qa.q: What did Saurabh put on the steel plate?
qa.a: A small heap of boiled peas.

qa.q: What does Deepak looking at his father after the first pea suggest?
qa.a: He seemed pleased with himself and maybe wanted Saurabh to notice his new trick.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try at the next meal to help Deepak practise?
qa.a: Offer small soft pieces again and plan extra time, since picking them up one by one is slow but good practice.

qa.q: What would change if Saurabh had fed Deepak with a spoon to save time?
qa.a: Lunch would be faster, but Deepak would lose the chance to practise his thumb-and-finger pinch.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from a whole-hand slap to a careful finger pinch while feeding himself.

passage:
"Jatin, give me the spoon," said Karthik, his big brother. "You're making a mess."
"No! Me!" Jatin gripped the spoon in his fist and plunged it into the curd rice.
"Amma, he's dropping more than he eats."
"Look how he's holding it now," Amma said from the stove. "Fingers, not the whole fist."
Jatin turned the spoon; half the rice fell, and the rest reached his mouth.
"He got it!" Karthik said. "Okay, okay. I'll hold the bowl still."
"Good idea," said Amma.

qa.q: What was Jatin eating?
qa.a: Curd rice.

qa.q: Why did Jatin shout "No! Me!" when Karthik asked for the spoon?
qa.a: He wanted to feed himself and felt determined, maybe cross, at the idea of his brother taking over.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Karthik holding the bowl still worked, because it helped Jatin keep practising instead of taking the spoon away.

qa.q: How does Karthik's view of Jatin change during the meal?
qa.a: He starts out annoyed by the mess, then cheers when Jatin succeeds and decides to help.

grounding: Shows a toddler refining his grip on a spoon while family members respond to the mess and the progress.

passage:
Note from Sonali, room teacher, 22 December
Today we made paper stars for the Christmas tree. Jaya stacked the wooden blocks into a tower of five before it fell, and she clapped. At the craft table she picked up sequins one at a time with her thumb and finger and pressed each onto the glue. When one stuck to her finger she shook her hand hard and frowned. I showed her how to wipe it on the paper, and she tried it twice. Tomorrow I'll put out bigger beads for threading 🙂

qa.q: How many blocks were in Jaya's tower before it fell?
qa.a: Five blocks were in the tower before it fell.

qa.q: What does Jaya's frown suggest when the sequin stuck to her finger?
qa.a: She seemed frustrated that the sequin wouldn't let go, since her careful pinching had stopped working.

qa.q: Why is Sonali's plan for bigger beads a good next step?
qa.a: It builds on the pinching Jaya is already doing and gives her a new task that is a little harder but still manageable.

qa.q: How might Jaya's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and pleased to see her small hand skills described in such detail.

grounding: Shows a toddler using a finger pinch and stacking blocks, noted by a teacher who plans the next step.

passage: Elif, two and a bit, wanted to walk the low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard. Liam, the student who babysat her on Wednesdays, held out a finger. She waved it away. Three steps in, she tipped left, bent her knees, flung her arms out, and stayed up. On the corner she tipped again and this time dropped onto her bottom in the sand, then climbed straight back on.

qa.q: Where was the edge that Elif walked along?
qa.a: The low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard.

qa.q: Why might Elif have waved Liam's finger away?
qa.a: She wanted to do it on her own and seemed confident enough to try without help.

qa.q: How could Liam support Elif on the sandpit edge without taking over?
qa.a: Stay close by, let her wobble and catch herself, and step in only if she is about to fall somewhere hard.

qa.q: What would change if the edge were next to concrete instead of sand?
qa.a: Liam would probably need to hold her hand, because a fall would hurt far more than dropping onto sand.

grounding: Shows a toddler shifting her weight on a narrow edge, catching herself with bent knees and arms, and recovering from a fall.

passage: I'm Afreen, and I watch my little cousin Hansa after school while her mother cooks. Yesterday Hansa was carrying her doll across the rug when her foot caught the edge. I thought she'd go flat on her face, but she threw one hand to the floor, bent low, and pushed herself back up without letting go of the doll. Later she squatted to pick up a crayon and stood again with no hands. I don't know if she was scared; she just kept walking.

qa.q: What was Hansa carrying across the rug?
qa.a: Her doll.

qa.q: What might Hansa have felt when her foot caught the rug?
qa.a: Maybe a quick fright, but she seemed calm and determined, since she caught herself and kept walking without crying.

qa.q: What could Afreen do to keep Hansa's practice safe at home?
qa.a: Keep the rug edges flat and the floor clear of sharp things, while still letting Hansa walk and squat freely.

qa.q: How does Afreen see what happened compared with what was expected?
qa.a: Afreen expected a hard fall, so it is a surprise that Hansa saved herself with one hand.

grounding: Shows a toddler catching herself mid-trip and squatting and standing without support, described by an older cousin.

passage: First day of the monsoon: Tejas, fourteen months, stood holding the window grille to watch the rain, and every time thunder cracked he sat down with a bump. His mother Rajni knelt beside him. Two weeks later: he stood watching without holding on, swaying as he turned to point at the puddles. The last week of the rains: he stepped from the doormat onto the wet verandah, slid, and caught himself on one knee before Rajni could reach him.

qa.q: What did Tejas hold while watching the rain on the first day?
qa.a: The window grille.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he sat down at each thunder crack?
qa.a: He was probably startled or a little scared, and sitting down felt safer than standing.

qa.q: How could Rajni help Tejas practise balance during the rainy weeks?
qa.a: Let him stand and turn near the window while wiping the wet verandah floor, so his slips happen on safe ground.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni when Tejas slides on the verandah?
qa.a: It is probably a jolt of worry, followed by relief that he caught himself on one knee.

grounding: Shows a toddler's balance growing over the monsoon, from holding on to standing free to catching himself on a slip.

passage: Keerthana stopped in the middle of the building's play area, crossed her legs and went very still. Her uncle Saurabh, visiting from Pune, didn't notice at first. "Susu," she said, tugging his kurta. "Susu now!" He grabbed her hand and ran for the lift. They made it, just. Back downstairs, she yawned, rubbed her eyes with both fists and climbed into his lap, the swing forgotten.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say while tugging Saurabh's kurta?
qa.a: She said, "Susu now!"

qa.q: What does Keerthana rubbing her eyes and climbing into Saurabh's lap suggest?
qa.a: She was tired and wanted comfort; her body's signals mattered more to her than the swing.

qa.q: What could Saurabh watch for next time he looks after Keerthana?
qa.a: Early signs like crossing her legs or going still, so he can take her to the toilet before it becomes urgent.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel after the rush to the lift?
qa.a: Relieved they made it in time, and maybe surprised at how clearly she told him what she needed.

grounding: Shows a toddler noticing and naming the need to use the toilet and later showing tiredness.

passage:
"Tummy," Vikas said, pressing his hand flat on his shirt.
"Your tummy hurts?" Vandana asked, putting down her laptop.
"No. Tummy empty."
She laughed. "Empty! You mean hungry?"
"Hungry. Banana."
"You had lunch an hour ago."
"Banana, Mummy." He leaned on her knee, eyes half shut.
"Hungry and sleepy, both?" she said. "Half a banana, then nap."
He ate it in four bites and was asleep on the mat before she had dropped the peel in the bin.

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vikas felt tired as well as hungry?
qa.a: He leaned on her knee with his eyes half shut and fell asleep right after eating, so he was sleepy and worn out.

qa.q: What did Vandana do well when Vikas said "tummy"?
qa.a: She stopped to ask what he meant instead of guessing, which helped him find the right word, hungry.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had refused the banana because lunch was recent?
qa.a: Vikas might have got upset and cranky, and he would learn that telling her his body's signals doesn't help.

grounding: Shows a toddler noticing hunger and tiredness in his body and finding words for them with his mother's help.

passage:
Creche note from Payal, a hot afternoon in May
Mehak came in from the shaded yard with red cheeks and went straight to the water jug, patting it and saying "paani, paani." She drank a full cup. After lunch she pulled at her dress and said "hot." I changed her into a cotton frock and put her mat under the fan. She was asleep in minutes. I've told her mother she is naming more of what her body feels now 😊

qa.q: What did Mehak say while patting the water jug?
qa.a: She said "paani, paani."

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she pulled at her dress and said "hot"?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and too warm, and she wanted Payal to fix it.

qa.q: How could Payal keep supporting Mehak's naming of body signals?
qa.a: Keep answering quickly when Mehak names a need, and give her words for new signals like "thirsty" or "sleepy".

qa.q: How might Mehak's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: Glad and reassured that Mehak is learning to tell carers what her body needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler recognising thirst, heat and tiredness on a summer day, noted by her carer.

passage: "Mehak, bring your shoes. We're going to the park." Manoj, her grandfather, said it once from the doorway. Mehak, fifteen months, who could only say "Nana" and "no", looked at him, looked at the shoe rack, toddled over and came back with one sandal and one of his slippers. He laughed and held up his own foot. "Yours, beta, not mine." She went back, dropped the slipper and returned with her second sandal.

qa.q: What did Mehak bring back the first time?
qa.a: One sandal and one of his slippers.

qa.q: Why did Mehak go back to the shoe rack a second time?
qa.a: She understood what her grandfather meant and wanted to get it right, and seemed pleased to help.

qa.q: How could Manoj keep building Mehak's understanding of words?
qa.a: Keep giving short, clear requests during daily routines and show her with gestures when she gets part of it wrong.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj to see her follow instructions she can't say yet?
qa.a: He finds it funny and delightful, and it shows him she understands far more than her two words.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a spoken instruction while she can say only two words.

passage:
"Sunaina, bath time. Can you put the duck in the bucket?" Deepak asked.
Sunaina, not yet talking, picked up the yellow duck and dropped it in with a splash.
"Now give Papa the towel."
She looked around, then pointed at the towel on the chair.
"Yes, that one. Can you bring it?"
She dragged it over, half on the floor.
"And where's the soap?"
She clapped her hands over her ears and ran to the bedroom, giggling.
"Ah. You understood that one too," Deepak said.

qa.q: What did Sunaina drop in the bucket?
qa.a: The yellow duck.

qa.q: What does Sunaina running away giggling at the word "soap" suggest?
qa.a: She clearly understood the word and felt playful and a bit mischievous, since she didn't want the bath yet.

qa.q: How could Deepak turn bath time into more listening practice?
qa.a: Keep giving one simple step at a time, like putting the duck in, and praise each step she follows.

qa.q: How does Deepak see Sunaina's giggling escape?
qa.a: He takes it with humour, as proof she understands "soap" even though she can't say it.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cannot yet talk understanding and acting on several spoken requests.

passage:
Playgroup note from Parveen, the week before Eid
Farida (20 months) still says only a few words, but she follows much more. Today I said, "Put the mehndi cones back in the box," and she did, one by one. When I said, "Wash hands, then snack," she walked to the tap first. She looked confused when I asked her to fetch "the blue one," so I pointed and she got it. I'll keep adding gestures to new words and share this with her family 🙂

qa.q: What did Farida put back in the box?
qa.a: The mehndi cones.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Parveen asked for "the blue one"?
qa.a: She seemed confused, perhaps unsure which item was meant, until Parveen pointed.

qa.q: Which choice by Parveen helped most, and why?
qa.a: Pointing when Farida got stuck, because it linked the new words to something she could see.

qa.q: How might Farida's family feel reading this note?
qa.a: Reassured that she understands a lot even though she talks little, and glad to know how to help.

grounding: Shows a toddler following two-step spoken instructions before she can say much herself.

passage: "Ba-ba-ba," Hansa used to shout at the goats. This week, standing in the courtyard with Nirmala, her Dadi, she pointed at the black kid goat and said, "Bakri." Then, when it nosed her hand: "Bakri, no!" Nirmala stopped sweeping. At the hand pump Hansa held out her tin cup and said, "Paani, Dadi, more." Nirmala filled it to the top and repeated each word back to her, slowly.

qa.q: What did Hansa call the black kid goat?
qa.a: She called it "Bakri."

qa.q: What might Nirmala have felt when she stopped sweeping?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and delighted to hear Hansa's first real words and a tiny sentence.

qa.q: How could Nirmala keep encouraging Hansa's talking?
qa.a: Keep repeating Hansa's words back clearly and adding one more word, so Hansa hears slightly longer phrases.

qa.q: What would change for Hansa if nobody answered her new words?
qa.a: She would get less reward for trying and might go back to pointing and shouting instead of talking.

grounding: Shows a toddler in a village moving from babbling to single words and short phrases to ask for what she needs.

passage: Kaito had spent months saying "da" for everything in the Madrid flat. On Tuesday he stood at the fridge, slapped the door, and said, "Milk." Lucia, his mother, froze with the kettle in her hand. "Milk? You want milk?" "Milk. Cup. Blue cup." She poured it into the blue cup. Kaito drank, set it down, and said, "More," very firmly, as if he had always been able to.

qa.q: What did Kaito ask for at the fridge?
qa.a: Milk, in the blue cup.

qa.q: Why did Lucia freeze with the kettle in her hand?
qa.a: She was surprised and thrilled to hear Kaito use real words after months of only saying "da". 😊

qa.q: How could Lucia build on this moment?
qa.a: Give him what he asks for when he uses words and repeat them back in short phrases, like "milk in the blue cup".

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito when his words finally get him what he wants?
qa.a: It likely feels powerful and satisfying, which is why he said "More" so firmly.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from a single babbled sound to words and short phrases that get his needs met.

passage: I'm Raghav, and on Holi morning I was in charge of my little brother Kunal while our parents greeted the neighbours. Last Holi he just babbled and screamed at the colours. This time he held up his wet hands and said, "Pink! Kunal pink!" When a water balloon burst near him, he shouted, "Bhaiya, again!" I can't tell what he meant by everything, but he talked all morning.

qa.q: What did Kunal shout when the water balloon burst?
qa.a: He shouted, "Bhaiya, again!"

qa.q: What does Kunal's "Bhaiya, again!" suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed excited and happy, wanting more of the fun instead of being scared by the burst.

qa.q: How could Raghav help Kunal keep using new words during the festival?
qa.a: Name the colours and actions back to him and wait for him to try, rather than answering for him.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the change in Kunal since last Holi?
qa.a: Raghav notices Kunal moving from babbling and screaming to short phrases, even if not every word is clear.

grounding: Shows a toddler's talk growing from babble to short phrases, seen by an older brother during a festival.

passage:
Note from Tejas, playgroup leader, Friday
We rolled a ball through the cardboard tunnel today. Pradeep (15 months) watched it go in, then turned his head to the far end before it came out, and squealed when it did. On the third roll I paused it inside; he stared at the exit, then crawled over to peek in. With the toy train he followed it round the whole track with his eyes. Next week: two tunnels.

qa.q: What did they roll through the cardboard tunnel?
qa.a: A ball.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's squeal when the ball came out suggest?
qa.a: He was delighted that it showed up where he expected, as if his guess had come true.

qa.q: Why might two tunnels be a good next step for Pradeep?
qa.a: It gives him a slightly harder guess about where the ball will appear, stretching his tracking without making it frustrating.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas never paused the ball inside?
qa.a: Tejas wouldn't have seen that Pradeep goes looking for it, which shows he knows it is still there.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a moving ball and train with his eyes and looking ahead to where the ball will come out.

passage: Every evening the goods train passed behind the sugarcane fields of their village, and Rekha carried her daughter Ankita to the edge of the yard to watch. At first Ankita only stared at the engine. Now, at twenty months, she follows it with her eyes until it slips behind the water tank, then swings her head to the other side of the tank and waits, pointing. When the engine appears again, she bounces in Rekha's arms and shouts, "Aa-gaya!"

qa.q: What does the train slip behind?
qa.a: The water tank.

qa.q: What does Ankita's pointing at the other side of the tank suggest?
qa.a: She expects the train to come out there and feels eager as she waits for it.

qa.q: How could Rekha play with this skill at home?
qa.a: Roll a ball behind a box and let Ankita guess where it will come out.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha to share this evening routine?
qa.a: It is likely a warm, happy moment, since she gets to see Ankita's new understanding up close.

grounding: Shows a toddler tracking a train with her eyes and looking ahead to where it will reappear.

passage: Snow had fallen overnight in Hamburg, and Esther pulled her grandson Felix, two, along the path on a small sled. A red bus crossed the end of the street and disappeared behind the bakery. Felix twisted round, eyes fixed on the far corner of the bakery, and held his breath. When the bus rolled out again he shouted "Bus!" and kicked his boots against the sled. Esther stopped so he could watch the next one.

qa.q: What did the red bus disappear behind?
qa.a: The bakery.

qa.q: Why did Felix hold his breath looking at the far corner?
qa.a: He expected the bus to reappear there and felt excited, waiting for it.

qa.q: How did Esther support Felix's interest, and what else could she try?
qa.a: She stopped so he could watch; she could also ask "Where will it come out?" to invite his guesses.

qa.q: How might Esther feel on this snowy walk?
qa.a: Probably amused and pleased to see him so absorbed, even if the walk takes longer.

grounding: Shows a toddler watching a bus vanish and looking ahead to where it will reappear on a winter walk.

passage: Bhavna's father Harsha was folding clothes on the bed in their Hyderabad flat when she crawled up with her rubber elephant. He dropped a towel over it. Bhavna, fourteen months, stared at the towel, then at him. She grabbed the corner, pulled, and found the elephant, squealing. He hid it again, this time under a pillow. She lifted the towel first, frowned, then lifted the pillow and grinned.

qa.q: Where did Harsha hide the elephant the second time?
qa.a: Under a pillow.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she found nothing under the towel?
qa.a: She seemed puzzled and a little frustrated, which shows she was sure the elephant was still somewhere.

qa.q: How could Harsha make this game a little harder next time?
qa.a: Hide the elephant under one of three cloths while she watches, so she has to follow where it went.

qa.q: What is it like for Harsha to play this game while folding?
qa.a: It turns a chore into a fun game, and he gets to watch her thinking at work.

grounding: Shows a toddler searching under a towel and then a pillow for a toy she knows is still there.

passage:
"Where's the ball, Ujjwal?" Jasleen asked, tucking it under the quilt.
Ujjwal looked at the lump. "Baw."
"Where did it go? Gone?"
He patted the quilt, found the lump, and pushed his hand underneath. "Baw!"
"You found it! Okay, now watch Didi." She slid it under the pillow instead.
He went straight back to the quilt, lifted it and frowned.
"Not there, is it?"
He stared at her hands, then at the pillow, and crawled towards it slowly.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen hide the ball first?
qa.a: Under the quilt.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's frown at the empty quilt suggest?
qa.a: He was confused and a little disappointed, since he expected the ball where he found it last time.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do to help Ujjwal succeed at the harder hiding?
qa.a: Hide it more slowly while he watches, and say "under the pillow" as she does it.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had just handed Ujjwal the ball?
qa.a: He'd get the toy, but he wouldn't practise searching for something he can't see.

grounding: Shows a toddler searching for a ball hidden under a quilt and working out where it moved.

passage:
Day-care note, Sachin, Lohri week
Because of the cold, we played indoors under shawls all morning. I hid a rattle under the red shawl while Akash (22 months) watched. He pulled it off right away. When I moved it under the blue shawl, he checked the red one first, then the blue. Later, on his own, he hid the rattle under his jumper and asked "Where?" with a big grin. I told his mother at pick-up; she laughed and said he hides her keys too.

qa.q: What did Sachin hide under the red shawl?
qa.a: A rattle.

qa.q: What does Akash's big grin when he hid the rattle suggest?
qa.a: He was proud and amused, enjoying turning the game around on Sachin.

qa.q: How could Akash's mother use this new game at home?
qa.a: She could hide his toys under a cloth for him to find, so the game stays fun and her keys stay safe.

qa.q: How does Sachin see Akash checking the red shawl first?
qa.a: As a normal step: Akash knows the rattle still exists but still looks where it was last.

grounding: Shows a toddler finding a rattle hidden under shawls and then hiding it himself, noted by a carer in winter.

passage: Harish came home from the office, dropped his bag, and blew one soap bubble over the sofa. His daughter Ganga, eighteen months, stopped chewing her biscuit. She watched it float, then chased it, and when it popped on her nose she shrieked with laughter and flapped both hands. "Again?" Harish asked. She slapped his knee. He blew ten more. She ran among them, spinning, until she sat down, dizzy and still giggling.

qa.q: Where did the bubble pop?
qa.a: On her nose.

qa.q: What does Ganga flapping her hands and shrieking suggest?
qa.a: She was delighted and excited by the bubble. 😊

qa.q: What small step could Harish keep in his routine?
qa.a: A few minutes of play like bubbles after work, following her lead, gives them a shared moment of joy.

qa.q: What might the bubbles mean for Harish after a long office day?
qa.a: Seeing her laugh probably lifts his own mood and helps him relax.

grounding: Shows a toddler's delight at a playful surprise from her father.

passage:
"Where's Chinmay? Where's he gone?" Elizabeth said, hands over her face.
Chinmay, in his high chair, held his breath.
"Boo!"
He squealed and banged the tray. "Gen! Gen!"
"Again? Okay. Where's Chinmay?" She pulled the tea towel over her own head this time.
He grabbed it and yanked it off, laughing so hard he hiccupped.
"Oh, you found Mummy!"
"Mumma boo!" he shouted, and held the towel out for her to wear again.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth pull over her head the second time?
qa.a: The tea towel.

qa.q: How can you tell Chinmay felt such delight in the game?
qa.a: He squealed, laughed until he hiccupped and handed the towel back, which shows real delight.

qa.q: How could Elizabeth keep the game fun for Chinmay?
qa.a: Let him take turns hiding her, as he started doing, so the play follows his lead.

qa.q: If you were Elizabeth, what would you enjoy most about this moment?
qa.a: Hearing him ask for more in his own words, "Mumma boo", and seeing how much the simple game delights him.

grounding: Shows a toddler's joyful reaction to a peekaboo game with his mother.

passage:
Nursery note by Yusuf, Diwali week
We hung paper lanterns and turned off the big lights for a shadow game. When I made a rabbit shadow on the wall, Eshaan (2) stared, then burst out laughing and ran to touch it. He tried to make his own and got a blob, which he found even funnier. He kept pulling my sleeve for "more bunny". A good day for him 😊 I'll show his parents how to do the rabbit at home.

qa.q: What shadow did Yusuf make on the wall?
qa.a: A rabbit shadow.

qa.q: What does Eshaan pulling Yusuf's sleeve for "more bunny" suggest?
qa.a: He was happy and wanted the fun to continue.

qa.q: Why is showing his parents the rabbit shadow a good idea?
qa.a: It lets them share the same playful moment at home with something simple.

qa.q: What would change if the big lights had stayed on?
qa.a: The shadows would barely show, so Eshaan would miss the surprise that made him laugh.

grounding: Shows a toddler's delight at a shadow game during a festival week, noted by his nursery teacher.

passage: Hiroshi arched his back like a bow the moment his mother Ines lowered him into the car seat outside the Lisbon supermarket. His face went red, his fists hammered the straps, and he howled, "No! No!" He had wanted to walk to the car on his own. Ines crouched by the door. "You're angry. You wanted to walk." He kicked once more, then hiccupped. She let him hold the car keys while she clicked the buckle.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi hammer with his fists?
qa.a: The straps of the car seat.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi arch his back and howl?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated because he wanted to walk to the car himself, not be strapped in. 😠

qa.q: Which choice by Ines helped, and why?
qa.a: Naming his feeling and giving him the keys calmed him, because he felt understood and had something to hold.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines to handle this outside a busy supermarket?
qa.a: It may feel stressful, but she stays calm and focused on him.

grounding: Shows a toddler's frustration when his movement is restricted, and a parent naming the feeling.

passage: I'm Bhavna, and I live next door to Kiran. Yesterday his grandmother was holding his hand at the gate so he couldn't run onto the road. Kiran pulled, dropped to the ground, and screamed until his face was wet. He threw his slipper. She didn't let go; she sat down on the step beside him and waited. I don't know exactly what he wanted, maybe the stray dog across the road. After a while he climbed into her lap.

qa.q: What did Kiran throw?
qa.a: His slipper.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling when he dropped to the ground?
qa.a: Frustrated and angry at being held back, especially if he wanted to reach the dog.

qa.q: What did the grandmother's approach get right?
qa.a: She kept him safe by not letting go, but stayed calm and waited beside him until he settled.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see the tantrum?
qa.a: Bhavna watches without judging and admits it is only a guess what Kiran wanted.

grounding: Shows a toddler's anger at being held back from the road, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Losar morning in Dharamshala: Tenzin, two, wanted to put on his new boots himself, jammed his foot in sideways, and threw them across the room, roaring. His father Imran picked him up and held him. Two days later: Tenzin pulled at a boot again, grunted, then pushed it towards Imran and said, "Help." A week after Losar: he got one boot on alone, stamped, and yelled, "Me did it!"

qa.q: What did Tenzin do with the boots on Losar morning?
qa.a: He threw them across the room.

qa.q: How can you tell Tenzin felt proud instead of angry by the end?
qa.a: He stamped and yelled "Me did it!", showing he felt proud once he managed alone.

qa.q: What could Imran do while Tenzin is learning to ask for help?
qa.a: Praise him for saying "Help" and do only the tricky part, so Tenzin still feels in charge.

qa.q: How might Imran feel as the week goes on?
qa.a: Relieved that the roaring has turned into asking for help, and pleased by Tenzin's success.

grounding: Shows a toddler's frustration when he can't manage his boots, changing over a week into asking for help and succeeding.
